title: ⭐⭐ Practice: whose words, and what the change of moment does to them

questions.prompt: Standing in the storeroom on the first of the month, the caretaker said to a pupil: "I am putting the new shelves up here tomorrow." A fortnight later, in the head teacher's office, the pupil passes those words on. Leaving the verb and the pronoun aside, which words of the caretaker's sentence can no longer be kept as they are, and why?

options.text: "here" only, because a word of time is fixed by the calendar and never moves.
"tomorrow" only, because a word of place is never touched in a report.
Neither of them: the words a person actually used must be kept exactly as they were said.
"here" and "tomorrow", because the report is made in another room and a fortnight later.

questions.explanation: Both words have to go, and for the same reason: here points at the place of the person speaking, and tomorrow at the day after the day she speaks. The pupil is now in the office and a fortnight has passed, so here would send the shelves to the wrong room and tomorrow would promise them for the wrong day. They become there and the next day. The line naming "here" only, because a word of time is fixed by the calendar and never moves, has it backwards: tomorrow names no date at all, it only counts one day from whoever is talking, which is exactly why it cannot be kept. The line naming "tomorrow" only, because a word of place is never touched in a report, states a rule that does not exist; here changes for the same reason tomorrow does. And "Neither of them: the words a person actually used must be kept exactly as they were said." describes direct speech, where the inverted commas do keep the exact words; a report has no inverted commas, and its job is to keep the sense true from where you now stand.

questions.prompt: A report on a school computer room says: "The machines are getting less and less reliable." Which of these four facts does that sentence record?

options.text: They break down more often than before, and the change is not over.
They have never been reliable at any moment of their life.
They broke down once, and that once was very bad.
They are less reliable than the machines of the school on the other side of town.

questions.explanation: "They break down more often than before, and the change is not over." is right: two comparatives joined by and record a movement that is under way and still going, and less and less points that movement downwards. "They have never been reliable at any moment of their life." denies that anything changed at all, whereas the sentence is entirely about a change. "They broke down once, and that once was very bad." replaces a movement with a single event; a doubled comparative can never describe one occasion. And "They are less reliable than the machines of the school on the other side of town." is what a plain comparative does, comparing two things at one moment; the doubled comparative compares the machines with themselves, earlier.

questions.prompt: During a visit to a workshop in Sousse, the engineer held a small green board up in front of the science club and said: "I designed this board myself." A month later Rania writes the visit up at home, for the school magazine: "The engineer said that she had designed ___ board herself." Which word fills the gap?

options.text: this
these
the
a

questions.explanation: "the" is right: this and these placed in front of a noun point at an object the speaker can hold up, and once the report is written a month later and somewhere else there is nothing left to point at, so the demonstrative gives way to the definite article. "this" keeps the pointing word in a sentence where no reader can follow the finger; it belongs inside the inverted commas the engineer used, not in the article. "these" adds a second fault to the first, since board is singular and these is plural. And "a" would present the board as a new thing the reader has never heard of, when the whole point of the sentence is that it is the one she held up.

questions.prompt: A science page for young readers ends on this line: "Nothing in the survey proves it, so the two researchers ___ that most families will own one screen for each child." Which word of the lesson fills the gap?

options.text: survive
assume
conceal
relieve

questions.explanation: "assume" is right: to assume is to take something as true when you have not proved it, and the first half of the sentence, nothing in the survey proves it, sets up exactly that situation. "survive" means to stay alive, or to come through a difficulty without being destroyed, and no difficulty is being come through here. "conceal" means to hide something on purpose so that others do not learn it; the researchers are publishing their idea, not hiding it. And "relieve" means to take away a pain or a worry, which is something you do to a person, not to a statement about the future.

questions.prompt: A school magazine prints this line about a visitor: "The engineer told the pupils that she had learned to code on a machine older than they were." Which of these four sentences is the one she actually said?

options.text: "I was learning to code on a machine older than you are."
"She learned to code on a machine older than they were."
"I learn to code on a machine older than you are."
"I learned to code on a machine older than you are."

questions.explanation: The sentence "I learned to code on a machine older than you are." is the one she said: you undo every change, one by one. The engineer speaking of herself says I, and speaking to the pupils in front of her says you; the were of the comparison goes back to are, since a present is what had stepped back to make it; and of the four sentences offered, the only one whose verb lands on had learned once the report is made in the past is the simple past, learned. The sentence "I was learning to code on a machine older than you are." puts the verb in the past continuous, and a past continuous reported after a past verb does not land on had learned at all: the magazine would then have printed that she had been learning to code. The sentence "She learned to code on a machine older than they were." leaves the third person in place, so the engineer would be speaking about somebody else and not about herself. And the sentence "I learn to code on a machine older than you are." puts the verb in the simple present, which a report in the past turns into a simple past and never sends further back than that.

questions.prompt: In the class debate on the human being of the future, Emna says: "In fifty years nobody will read a paper book, and nobody will remember how to write by hand." Wassim thinks the first half is worth discussing but that the second goes far too far, and he does not want to throw away everything she said. Which reply does exactly that?

options.text: You are right about the books, but the rest of it goes much too far.
That is exactly it, and there is not a word of it I would change.
You are wrong from the first word to the last, and the whole class can see it.
I would rather not take a side on a question of that kind at all.

questions.explanation: "You are right about the books, but the rest of it goes much too far." is the reply: it keeps what is defensible in Emna's sentence, what may become of paper books, and refuses only what is excessive, a world in which nobody can write by hand. That double move, granting one half and then marking the limit, is what disagreeing properly looks like in a debate, and it is stronger than a flat no because the other speaker has nothing left to defend. "That is exactly it, and there is not a word of it I would change." agrees with the whole of it, including the very part Wassim rejects. "You are wrong from the first word to the last, and the whole class can see it." throws away the books along with the rest and answers with a crowd instead of an argument. And "I would rather not take a side on a question of that kind at all." is a refusal to speak: Wassim has an opinion, and this sentence hides it.
